Absolute Extrema
section.paragraph: The graph of the function $$f$$ in Figure 56 shows the average age of cars in use in the United States from the beginning of 1946 $$\left( {t = 0} \right)$$ to the beginning of 2009 $$\left( {t = 63} \right)$$ . Observe that the highest average age of cars in use during this period is $$9.3$$ years, whereas the lowest average age of cars in use during the same period is $$5.5$$ years. The number $$9.3$$ , the largest value of $$f(t)$$ for all values of $$t$$ in the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,63} \right\rbrack$$ (the domain of $$f$$ ), is called the absolute maximum value of $$f$$ on that interval. The number $$5.5$$ , the smallest value of $$f(t)$$ for all values of $$t$$ in $$\left\lbrack {0,63} \right\rbrack$$ , is called the absolute minimum value of $$f$$ on that interval. Notice, too, that the absolute maximum value of $$f$$ is attained at the endpoint $$t = 63$$ of the interval, whereas the absolute minimum value of $$f$$ is attained at the points $$t = 12$$ (corresponding to 1958) and $$t = 23$$ (corresponding to 1969) that lie within the interval $$\left( {0,63} \right)$$ .

A precise definition of the absolute extrema (absolute maximum or absolute minimum) of a function follows.

note.source_type: The Absolute Extrema of a Function f
note.title: The Absolute Extrema of a Function f
note.heading: The Absolute Extrema of a Function f
note.paragraph: If $$f(x) \leq f(c)$$ for all $$x$$ in the domain of $$f$$ , then $$f(c)$$ is called the absolute maximum value of $$f$$ .
If $$f(x) \geq f(c)$$ for all $$x$$ in the domain of $$f$$ , then $$f(c)$$ is called the absolute minimum value of $$f$$ .

section.heading: Absolute Extrema on a Closed Interval
section.paragraph: As the preceding examples show, a continuous function defined on an arbitrary interval does not always have an absolute maximum or an absolute minimum. But an important case arises often in practical applications in which both the absolute maximum and the absolute minimum of a function are guaranteed to exist. This occurs when a continuous function is defined on a closed interval.

Before stating this important result formally, let’s look at a real-life example. The graph of the function $$f$$ in Figure 58 shows the average price, $$f(t)$$ , in dollars, of domestic airfares by days before flight. The domain of $$f$$ is the closed interval $$\lbrack - 210, - 1\rbrack$$ , where $$- 210$$ is interpreted as $$210$$ days before flight and $$- 1$$ is interpreted as the day before flight.

image.alt: Details A curve is graphed on a coordinate plane. The horizontal axis t is marked from negative 200 to 0 in increments of 50 days. The vertical axis y is marked from 300 to 700 in increments of 100 dollars. There is an axis breaker just below the mark 300 on the vertical axis. The curve begins with a filled dot at (negative 200, 550), descends gradually to the right, concave up, reaching a low point at (negative 50, 400), and then rises upward rapidly to the right, till around (negative 5, 600) where it ends with a filled dot.

section.paragraph: Observe that $$f$$ attains the minimum value of $$395$$ when $$t = - 49$$ and the maximum value of $$614$$ when $$t = - 1$$ . This result tells us that the best time to book a domestic flight is seven weeks in advance and the worst day to book a domestic flight is the day before the flight. Probably most surprising of all, booking too early can be almost as expensive as booking too late. Note that the function $$f$$ is continuous on a closed interval. For such functions, we have the following theorem.

note.title: Theorem 3
note.heading: Theorem 3
note.paragraph: If a function $$f$$ is continuous on a closed interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ , then $$f$$ has both an absolute maximum value and an absolute minimum value on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ .

section.paragraph: Observe that if an absolute extremum of a continuous function $$f$$ occurs at a point in an open interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then it must be a relative extremum of $$f$$ , and hence its $$x$$ -coordinate must be a critical number of $$f$$ . Otherwise, the absolute extremum of $$f$$ must occur at one or both of the endpoints of the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . A typical situation is illustrated in Figure 59.

image.alt: Details A curve y = f(x) is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis has marks labeled a, x_1, x_2, x_3, and b, appear at unequal intervals. From each of these marks a vertical line, parallel to the y axis rises upward to meet the graph. The y axis is unmarked. The curve begins with a filled dot from the top left, a short distance from the y axis. A vertical line connects the filled dot to the mark a on the x axis. The curve then descends to the right, concave up, reaches a low point, marked with a filled dot and labeled Relative minimum. A vertical line connects the filled dot to the mark x_1 on the x axis. From the relative minimum, the curve rises a bit more steeply to the right, concave up, to reach a high point marked with a filled dot and labeled relative maximum. A vertical line connects the filled dot to the mark x_2 on the x axis. The graph then descends gradually to the right, concave up, and reaches a low point, below all other marked points, marked with a filled dot and labeled Absolute minimum. A vertical line connects the filled dot to the mark x_3 on the x axis. From there the curve rises upward to the right, inflects, and then continues to rise to the right, now concave down till it reaches a point above all other marked points. This point is marked with a filled dot and labeled Absolute maximum. A vertical line connects the filled dot to the mark b on the x axis.

figure.caption: The relative minimum of $$f$$ at $$x_{3}$$ is the absolute minimum of $$f$$ . The right endpoint $$b$$ of the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ gives rise to the absolute maximum value $$f(b)$$ of $$f$$

section.paragraph: Here, $$x_{1}$$ , $$x_{2}$$ , and $$x_{3}$$ are critical numbers of $$f$$ . The absolute minimum of $$f$$ occurs at $$x_{3}$$ , which lies in the open interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ and is a critical number of $$f$$ . The absolute maximum of $$f$$ occurs at $$b$$ , an endpoint. This observation suggests the following procedure for finding the absolute extrema of a continuous function on a closed interval.

section.paragraph: Many real-world applications call for finding the absolute maximum value or the absolute minimum value of a given function. For example, management is interested in finding what level of production will yield the maximum profit for a company; a farmer is interested in finding the right amount of fertilizer to maximize crop yield; a doctor is interested in finding the maximum concentration of a drug in a patient’s body and the time at which it occurs; and an engineer is interested in finding the dimensions of a container with a specified shape and volume that can be constructed at a minimum cost.

note.title: Applied Example 5. Trachea Contraction during a Cough
note.heading: Applied Example 5. Trachea Contraction during a Cough
note.paragraph: When a person coughs, the trachea (windpipe) contracts, allowing air to be expelled at a maximum velocity. It can be shown that during a cough, the velocity $$\nu$$ of airflow is given by the function
$$v = f(r) = kr^{2}\left( {R - r} \right)$$

where $$r$$ is the trachea’s radius (in centimeters) during a cough, $$R$$ is the trachea’s normal radius (in centimeters), and $$k$$ is a positive constant that depends on the length of the trachea. Find the radius $$r$$ for which the velocity of airflow is greatest.
note.heading: Solution
note.paragraph: To find the absolute maximum of $$f$$ on $$\left\lbrack {0,R} \right\rbrack$$ , first find the critical numbers of $$f$$ on the interval $$\left( {0,R} \right)$$ . We compute
$$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(r)} = {2kr\left( {R - r} \right) - kr^{2}} {Use the Product Rule.}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(r)} = {- 3kr^{2} + 2kRr = kr\left( {- 3r + 2R} \right)}} \end{array}$$

Setting $$f^{\prime}(r) = 0$$ gives $$r = 0$$ or $$r = \frac{2}{3}R$$ , so $$\frac{2}{3}R$$ is the sole critical number of $$f$$ ( $$r = 0$$ is an endpoint). Evaluating $$f(r)$$ at $$r = \frac{2}{3}R$$ , as well as at the endpoints $$r = 0$$ and $$r = R$$ , we obtain
$$\begin{array}{rcl} {f(0)} & = & 0 \\ {f\left( {\frac{2}{3}R} \right)} & = & {\frac{4k}{27}R^{3}} \\ {f(R)} & = & 0 \end{array}$$

from which we deduce that the velocity of airflow is greatest when the radius of the contracted trachea is $$\frac{2}{3}R$$ —that is, when the radius is contracted by approximately $$33\%$$ . The graph of the function $$f$$ is shown in Figure 64.

Similarly, using the function for finding the absolute maximum value, we find the absolute maximum value to be $$4.1593$$ .

note.title: Note
note.heading: Note
note.paragraph: Some graphing utilities will enable you to find the absolute minimum and absolute maximum values of a continuous function on a closed interval without having to graph the function. For example, using fMax on the TI-83/84 will yield the $$x$$ -coordinate of the absolute maximum of $$f$$ . The absolute maximum value can then be found by evaluating $$f$$ at that value of $$x$$ . Figure T2 shows the work involved in finding the absolute maximum of the function of Example 1.
